lead: Data communication moves binary bits from a source that creates the information to a destination that uses it. The movement needs a transmitter to turn bits into a signal, a physical channel that carries the signal, and a receiver that reconverts the signal back to bits. Understanding these five parts and how they can exchange data in one or both directions is the basis for every network protocol and device, from a cheap IoT sensor to a high‑speed telecom backbone.

sections.h3: Basic components of a data‑communication system

blocks.text: A data‑communication system is built from five logical blocks. The **Source** generates the data bits. The **Transmitter** encodes the bits into a waveform suitable for the medium. The **Channel** is the physical path – copper wire, fiber, or air – that carries the waveform. The **Receiver** decodes the waveform back into bits. The **Destination** consumes the bits as useful information. Each block can be implemented by hardware, software, or a combination of both.

items: Source – e.g., a temperature sensor, a web server, or a user’s keyboard.
Transmitter – e.g., a UART, a modem, or a network interface card.
Channel – e.g., a twisted‑pair cable, an optical fiber, or a wireless link.
Receiver – e.g., a demodulator, a PHY chip, or a software driver.
Destination – e.g., a data logger, a computer, or a display.

blocks.text: These components appear in every networking standard. In the OSI model they map roughly to the Physical layer (transmitter, channel, receiver) and the upper layers (source, destination). See OSI reference model for the layer mapping.
Syllabi describe the direction of data flow with three terms. They indicate how many logical channels exist between the two ends.

items: Simplex – data moves only from source to destination. Example: a TV broadcast.
Half‑duplex – a single channel is shared; data can travel both ways but not at the same time. Example: walkie‑talkie.
Full‑duplex – two independent channels allow simultaneous two‑way transfer. Example: a telephone conversation.

blocks.text: Choosing the mode influences protocol design. Full‑duplex links need separate buffers for each direction, while simplex links can omit the reverse path entirely, saving cost.

items: Identify the source and the destination of the information.
Select a transmitter that can encode the data for the chosen channel.
Pick a channel whose bandwidth meets the required data rate.
Choose a receiver compatible with the transmitter’s signal format.
Decide the direction mode (simplex, half‑duplex, full‑duplex) based on application needs.

blocks.text: For a smart‑meter reading sent to a utility server, the meter is the source, a cellular modem is the transmitter, the air‑interface is the channel, the base‑station receiver is the receiver, and the server is the destination. The link is usually full‑duplex so the server can acknowledge receipt.

examples.question: A sensor sends 500 bytes to a server over a 1 Mbps full‑duplex link. Compute the transmission time required to push the entire frame onto the channel. Assume no propagation delay and no protocol overhead.
steps: Convert bytes to bits: 500 bytes × 8 bits/byte = 4000 bits.
Data rate of the link: 1 Mbps = 1 000 000 bits/s.
Transmission time = total bits ÷ data rate = 4000 bits ÷ 1 000 000 bits/s = 0.004 s.
examples.check:
bits = 500 * 8
rate = 1_000_000
time = bits / rate
print(time)

traps: Adding the transmission time for both directions in a full‑duplex link and then doubling the result.
Using kilobits (kb) instead of kilobits per second (kbps) and forgetting the per‑second factor.
Treating the 500 bytes as 500 bits, which reduces the computed time by a factor of eight.
Including propagation delay when the question explicitly says to ignore it.

quiz.q: Name the five logical blocks of a data‑communication system.
Explain why a full‑duplex link needs two separate buffers at each end.
quiz.a: Because data can travel simultaneously in both directions, each direction must have its own storage to hold incoming frames while the other direction is being transmitted.

quiz.q: A webcam streams 2 MiB of video every second over a 10 Mbps link. Is the link sufficient? Show your calculation.
quiz.a: Convert 2 MiB to bits: 2 × 2^20 bytes × 8 = 16 777 216 bits. Required rate = 16 777 216 bits/s ≈ 16.78 Mbps, which exceeds 10 Mbps, so the link is insufficient.

quiz.q: If a half‑duplex radio uses a 500 kHz channel with a data rate of 250 kbps, how long does it take to send a 1 KB packet assuming no overhead?
quiz.a: 1 KB = 1024 bytes = 8192 bits. Time = 8192 bits ÷ 250 000 bits/s = 0.032768 s ≈ 32.8 ms.

quiz.q: Compare simplex and half‑duplex modes in terms of hardware cost and protocol complexity.
quiz.a: Simplex needs only a transmitter at one end and a receiver at the other, reducing hardware cost. Protocols are simpler because no coordination for reverse traffic is required. Half‑duplex adds a single shared channel, requiring additional logic for turn‑taking (e.g., CSMA) and possibly extra transceiver circuitry, increasing both cost and complexity.

quiz.q: What term describes the direction of data flow when both ends can send simultaneously?
Why does a full‑duplex link not double the effective bandwidth of a single‑direction channel?
quiz.a: Because each direction uses its own separate channel; the bandwidth of each direction remains the same as the single‑direction channel. The total aggregate capacity is doubled, but the per‑direction capacity does not increase.

beyond: Not for the exam. In modern data‑centers, full‑duplex optical links at 100 Gbps dominate, and software‑defined networking can re‑configure direction modes on demand. Research on in‑band full‑duplex radios seeks to transmit and receive on the same frequency simultaneously, promising spectral efficiency gains. Emerging curricula add a dedicated module on physical‑layer security, covering jamming and covert channels. To explore further, search for "full‑duplex wireless" and "software‑defined networking data‑plane".
